screens.title: Nmap for Initial AD Reconnaissance
screens.narratorSegment: We begin our practical enumeration journey with nmap, a versatile network scanner that is invaluable for initial reconnaissance. While nmap is a general-purpose tool, it's particularly effective for identifying services running on potential Domain Controllers or other Windows machines within an Active Directory environment. Beyond simply scanning standard AD ports like 88 for Kerberos, 135 for RPC, 139 and 445 for SMB, 389 for LDAP, and 636 for LDAPS, nmap truly shines when combined with its powerful scripting engine. For instance, the smb-enum-users script can attempt to enumerate valid user accounts via the SMB protocol, while ldap-search can perform basic LDAP queries to gather initial directory information. A common nmap command for initial AD reconnaissance, as shown on screen, targets these crucial ports and leverages scripts to provide a rich initial dataset. A frequent mistake here is to run nmap without these specific AD-focused scripts, which means you'd miss out on a wealth of valuable initial enumeration data that could quickly point you towards potential vulnerabilities. Always remember to tailor your nmap scans to the specific context of Active Directory.

Module 9.2›Chapter 9.2›Nmap for Initial AD Reconnaissance
TOOL FOCUS

Nmap for Initial AD Reconnaissance

Identifying Services and Basic Information

nmap -p 53,88,135,139,389,445,464,636,3268,3269 \
     --script "smb-enum-users,ldap-search,smb-os-discovery" \
     -sV <DC_IP>
Common Mistake

Running Nmap without specific AD scripts misses valuable initial enumeration data.

Key Takeaway

Leverage Nmap's script engine with AD-specific scripts to gain deep initial insights into services and potential user accounts.

Target AD Ports

Scan common AD ports (88, 135, 139, 389, 445, 636) to identify core services.

Leverage Nmap Scripts

Identify OS & Services

The `-sV` flag and `smb-os-discovery` script help identify the operating system and service versions.

screens.title: Targeted Enumeration with Enum4linux
screens.narratorSegment: Once we've identified potential Windows servers and their open ports using nmap, our next step is to move to more targeted enumeration, especially from a Linux-based attack machine. For this, enum4linux is an indispensable tool. It's specifically designed to enumerate information from Windows and Samba hosts, leveraging various techniques to extract valuable data. One of its core methods is NetBIOS enumeration, which can reveal hostnames, domain names, and workgroup information. More powerfully, enum4linux employs RID cycling, a technique that iterates through Relative Identifiers to guess valid user accounts. It also utilizes the Security Account Manager Remote (SAMR) protocol to enumerate users and groups. Running enum4linux -a against a target IP, as shown on screen, will attempt to perform all available enumeration techniques, often revealing extensive lists of users, groups, and shared resources. While this can sometimes be a noisy operation, it's an excellent first pass for gathering critical intelligence. For example, using enum4linux -U specifically targets user enumeration, which is a significant step forward for potential password spraying or brute-force attacks. Identifying valid usernames is a cornerstone of many AD attack vectors, making enum4linux a vital tool in your arsenal.

Targeted Enumeration with Enum4linux

Extracting Users, Groups, and Shares from Linux

Consideration

Key Takeaway

RID Cycling

Iterates through Relative Identifiers (RIDs) to guess valid user accounts, a core technique for user enumeration.

User & Group Enumeration

screens.title: Querying Active Directory via LDAP
screens.narratorSegment: While nmap and enum4linux provide valuable initial insights, the real power of Active Directory enumeration comes from direct interaction with the LDAP service. LDAP, or Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, is the primary protocol used to query and modify the AD database, offering access to a vast amount of information. On Linux, ldapsearch is your go-to command-line tool for this. To use it effectively, you'll need to know the base Distinguished Name, or DN, of the domain, which is typically derived from the domain name itself. For example, for a domain named corp. local, the base DN would be dc equals corp,dc equals local. As you see on screen, a basic query can list all user accounts by filtering for objects of class user and requesting specific attributes like s AMAccount Name. You can refine these filters to find specific groups, computers, or users with interesting attributes. For instance, filtering for admin Count equals 1 can reveal administrative users, while service Principal Name equals asterisk identifies users or computers with Service Principal Names, which are prime targets for Kerberoasting attacks. Understanding how to craft precise LDAP filters is crucial for extracting highly targeted intelligence from Active Directory.

keyIdea.title: LDAP: Direct AD Access
keyIdea.text: `ldapsearch` allows direct, granular querying of the Active Directory database via LDAP, enabling the discovery of specific objects and attributes crucial for exploitation.

content.html:
Module 9.2›Chapter 9.2›Querying Active Directory via LDAP
PROTOCOL EXPLOITATION

Querying Active Directory via LDAP

Leveraging ldapsearch for Detailed Information

# List all user accounts
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<DC_IP> -b "dc=corp,dc=local" "(objectClass=user)" sAMAccountName

# Find administrative users
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<DC_IP> -b "dc=corp,dc=local" "(adminCount=1)" sAMAccountName

# Identify users with SPNs
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<DC_IP> -b "dc=corp,dc=local" "(&(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*))" sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName
Important Note

Anonymous LDAP binds (`-x`) may be disabled in hardened environments, requiring authentication.

Key Takeaway

`ldapsearch` provides granular control over AD queries, allowing you to extract specific object attributes vital for identifying attack vectors like Kerberoasting targets.

LDAP Protocol

The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol is the primary method for querying and modifying Active Directory data.

Base DN

The Distinguished Name (DN) specifies the starting point for an LDAP search within the directory tree.

LDAP Filters

Powerful syntax to specify criteria for selecting objects, enabling highly targeted queries.

screens.title: PowerShell: The Native AD Enumeration Tool
screens.narratorSegment: For Windows-based attack machines, or once you've established a foothold within a domain, PowerShell becomes an incredibly powerful and often stealthier tool for Active Directory enumeration. The Active Directory module, which can be imported using Import-Module Active Directory, provides a comprehensive suite of cmdlets specifically designed for interacting with AD. These cmdlets, such as Get-ADUser, Get-ADGroup, Get-ADComputer, Get-ADDomain, and Get-ADForest, allow for highly granular and efficient querying of the AD database directly from a Windows host. As you can see in the examples on screen, you can retrieve all user accounts and display selected properties like s AMAccount Name, Description, and Enabled with a simple Get-ADUser command. Furthermore, PowerShell excels at finding specific attributes, such as users with Service Principal Names, which are crucial for Kerberoasting attacks. You can achieve this by filtering for users where Service Principal Name is not null. These PowerShell cmdlets are often preferred in post-exploitation scenarios due to their native integration, which can be less conspicuous than external tools, and their ability to perform complex queries with ease. Mastering PowerShell for AD enumeration is a key skill for any advanced penetration tester.

keyIdea.text: PowerShell's `ActiveDirectory` module provides native, powerful, and stealthy cmdlets for granular enumeration of AD objects and attributes from Windows hosts.

content.html:
Module 9.2›Chapter 9.2›PowerShell: The Native AD Enumeration Tool
NATIVE ENUMERATION

PowerShell: The Native AD Enumeration Tool

Leveraging ActiveDirectory Cmdlets for Precision

# Import the ActiveDirectory module
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Get all domain users with selected properties
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Description,Enabled | \
    Select-Object Name,sAMAccountName,Description,Enabled

# Find users with Service Principal Names (SPNs)
Get-ADUser -Filter 'ServicePrincipalName -ne "$null"' -Properties ServicePrincipalName | \
    Select-Object Name,sAMAccountName,ServicePrincipalName
Prerequisite

The ActiveDirectory module must be installed, typically part of RSAT tools or on a Domain Controller.

Key Takeaway

PowerShell cmdlets offer a powerful, efficient, and stealthy way to perform detailed Active Directory enumeration from within a Windows environment.

Native Integration

PowerShell is built into Windows, making it a natural and often less detectable tool for AD interaction.

Granular Cmdlets

Specific cmdlets like `Get-ADUser` or `Get-ADGroup` allow precise querying of AD objects and their properties.

Post-Exploitation Value

Ideal for detailed enumeration and privilege escalation once initial access to a Windows host is gained.

screens.title: BloodHound: Mapping Complex Attack Paths
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond individual enumeration tools, the Blood Hound analysis tool is an absolute game-changer for Active Directory enumeration and attack path mapping. Imagine trying to manually trace every possible connection between users, groups, computers, and their permissions in a large AD environment; it would be nearly impossible. Blood Hound solves this by collecting vast amounts of data from an AD environment—including users, groups, computers, Access Control Lists, Group Policy Objects, and active sessions—and then visualizes these relationships within a graph database. This powerful visualization allows penetration testers to quickly identify complex, multi-step attack paths that might lead directly to domain administrative privileges. The data collection typically involves running a PowerShell ingestor script, such as Sharp Hound. ps1, or a C# executable like Blood Hound. exe, on a compromised host within the target domain. Once collected, this JSON data is imported into the Blood Hound GUI, which runs on a Neo4j database. Blood Hound can then reveal intricate paths, for example, showing how 'User A is a member of Group B, which has local admin rights on Computer C, where User D is logged in, and User D is a member of Domain Admins.' Understanding these complex, often hidden, relationships is absolutely critical for planning effective lateral movement and privilege escalation strategies. It transforms a chaotic data dump into an actionable attack map.

screens.title: A Systematic Approach to AD Enumeration (Part 1)
screens.narratorSegment: When performing Active Directory enumeration, it's absolutely crucial to be systematic. A haphazard approach will inevitably lead to missed opportunities and wasted time. We always recommend starting broad and then progressively narrowing your focus. The first step in this systematic approach is to identify Domain Controllers. These are the heart of your Active Directory environment, and knowing their IP addresses is fundamental. You can achieve this using tools like nmap or by querying DNS records. Once you've identified your Domain Controllers, the second step is to enumerate users and groups. This is where tools like enum4linux, ldapsearch, or PowerShell's Get-ADUser and Get-ADGroup cmdlets come into play. During this phase, you should actively look for naming conventions, identify any disabled accounts that might still hold privileges, and, most importantly, pinpoint privileged groups like 'Domain Admins' or 'Enterprise Admins'. The third step involves enumerating computers within the domain. This helps you identify potential targets for lateral movement or machines running specific services that could be vulnerable. Understanding the landscape of machines is just as important as understanding the users. By following these initial steps, you lay a solid foundation for deeper enumeration and attack planning.

screens.title: A Systematic Approach to AD Enumeration (Part 2)
screens.narratorSegment: Continuing our systematic approach, once you have a foundational understanding of the core Active Directory assets, it's time to dig deeper into relationships and potential misconfigurations. Step four involves identifying trust relationships. These trusts, which can be discovered using PowerShell's Get-ADTrust cmdlet, reveal connections between different domains or even entire forests. Understanding these trusts is crucial because they often indicate potential lateral movement paths, allowing an attacker to pivot from one trusted domain to another. The fifth step is to actively look for Service Principal Names, or SPNs. These are unique identifiers for service instances used by Kerberos authentication, and they are associated with either user or computer accounts. SPNs are critical because they are prime targets for Kerberoasting attacks, where an attacker can request a service ticket for an SPN and then attempt to crack its associated password offline. Finally, step six focuses on analyzing Access Control Lists, or ACLs, and Group Policy Objects, or GPOs. While Blood Hound is excellent for visualizing these, cmdlets like Get-ACL and Get-GPO can also provide valuable insights into permissions and configurations that might lead to privilege escalation. Remember, the more information you gather, the higher your chances of finding a vulnerability, so don't stop enumeration too early.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices in AD Enumeration
screens.narratorSegment: As you become more proficient in Active Directory enumeration, it's important to be aware of common pitfalls and adhere to best practices. One of the most frequent mistakes is stopping enumeration too early. The more information you gather, the higher your chances of finding a vulnerability. It's a process of continuous discovery, and often, the most valuable insights are hidden deep within the directory. Another significant mistake is being too noisy. Some enumeration techniques can generate a lot of network traffic or trigger alerts within a security operations center, potentially revealing your presence prematurely. Always consider the potential impact of your actions and strive for stealth when possible. For safety and ethical reasons, always perform these activities in a controlled lab environment. Never conduct real-world engagements without explicit, written authorization. Effective enumeration isn't just about running tools; it's about understanding the output, correlating information from various sources, and building a comprehensive mental model of the target's Active Directory. This holistic understanding allows you to identify logical attack paths and exploit vulnerabilities strategically, rather than blindly. Remember, patience and precision are your greatest allies in this phase.

Common Mistakes in AD Enumeration

Pitfalls to Avoid for Effective Reconnaissance

Stopping Too Early

Prematurely ending enumeration can lead to missed vulnerabilities and attack paths.

Being Too Noisy

Aggressive scanning can trigger alerts and reveal your presence to defenders.

Lack of Authorization

Never perform enumeration on systems without explicit, written permission.

Best Practices for AD Enumeration

Maximizing Effectiveness While Minimizing Risk

Be Systematic & Thorough

Follow a structured approach from broad scans to targeted queries to ensure comprehensive data collection.

Understand the Output

Don't just run tools; interpret the results and correlate information to build a mental model of the AD.

Practice in Labs

Hone your skills in controlled lab environments to avoid unintended consequences in real engagements.

Effective AD enumeration balances thoroughness with discretion, requiring a deep understanding of the environment and strict adherence to ethical guidelines and authorization.

Foundational Terms in AD Reconnaissance

Reconnaissance

The initial phase of gathering information about a target, often passively, to understand its landscape.

Enumeration

The active process of extracting detailed information about a target, such as users, groups, shares, and services.

RID Cycling

Reconnaissance and enumeration are distinct but complementary phases, with techniques like RID Cycling providing specific methods for intelligence gathering.

Welcome to Chapter 9.2, where we'll dive deep into Active Directory Reconnaissance and Enumeration. This phase is absolutely critical for any successful penetration test targeting an Active Directory environment. Think of it like being a detective: before you can solve a mystery, you need to gather all the clues. In AD, these clues are user accounts, groups, computers, and their intricate relationships. Without a clear understanding of this landscape, any attempt to exploit vulnerabilities would be like stumbling in the dark, highly inefficient and likely to fail. Our goal is to systematically paint a complete picture of the AD structure, identifying potential weak points, misconfigurations, and valuable targets that will guide our subsequent attack phases. This process can be time-consuming, but the intelligence gathered here yields the highest returns in terms of identifying viable attack paths and achieving our objectives.

In this chapter, we'll focus on developing practical skills essential for any penetration tester working with Active Directory. Our first objective is to equip you with the ability to execute various reconnaissance techniques. This means you'll learn how to discover crucial Active Directory domain information, such as domain names, valid user accounts, security groups, and computer objects. Understanding these foundational elements is like getting the lay of the land before a mission. Secondly, we'll dive into utilizing common enumeration tools. You'll become proficient with tools like nmap for initial network scans, enum4linux for targeted host enumeration, ldapsearch for direct LDAP queries, and Power View for powerful PowerShell-based intelligence gathering. These tools are your primary instruments for extracting valuable data from an AD environment, and mastering them is key to effective information gathering.

Continuing our journey, our third objective is to identify and interpret key attributes of Active Directory objects. This goes beyond just listing users; it's about understanding what specific properties, like admin Count or service Principal Name, signify and how they can be leveraged in later attack phases. For example, knowing an account has an SPN immediately flags it as a potential Kerberoasting target. Fourth, you will understand the critical role of core network protocols like DNS, SMB, and LDAP in the enumeration process. We'll explore how their inherent functionalities can be exploited to gather intelligence, from querying DNS records to enumerating shares via SMB or directly querying the directory via LDAP. Finally, we'll synthesize all this knowledge to formulate a systematic approach to AD enumeration. This means progressing from broad network scans to highly targeted queries, ensuring you don't miss crucial details and can efficiently map out the entire Active Directory environment. This structured methodology is what separates a haphazard attempt from a professional, effective penetration test.

Having grasped the fundamentals of Active Directory, our next crucial step as penetration testers is to effectively enumerate and gather information from it. Reconnaissance and enumeration are not just preliminary steps; they are the absolute bedrock of any successful AD attack. Imagine trying to navigate a complex building in the dark without a map; that's what attempting exploitation without proper enumeration feels like. Our primary goal in this phase is to paint as complete a picture as possible of the AD structure. This includes identifying all its users, groups, computers, and, most importantly, the relationships between them. This detailed understanding allows us to pinpoint potential weak points, uncover misconfigurations, and identify valuable targets that can lead to privilege escalation or lateral movement. While this phase can often be time-consuming, the intelligence it yields in terms of identifying viable attack paths is unparalleled and ultimately saves significant time in later exploitation stages. It's about working smarter, not just harder, to achieve your objectives. Why Active Directory Enumeration Matters means comprehensive ad enumeration provides the essential intelligence to identify vulnerabilities and map out effective attack paths, preventing blind exploitation attempts.. In practical terms, building the blueprint for successful exploitation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We begin our practical enumeration journey with nmap, a versatile network scanner that is invaluable for initial reconnaissance. While nmap is a general-purpose tool, it's particularly effective for identifying services running on potential Domain Controllers or other Windows machines within an Active Directory environment. Beyond simply scanning standard AD ports like 88 for Kerberos, 135 for RPC, 139 and 445 for SMB, 389 for LDAP, and 636 for LDAPS, nmap truly shines when combined with its powerful scripting engine. For instance, the smb-enum-users script can attempt to enumerate valid user accounts via the SMB protocol, while ldap-search can perform basic LDAP queries to gather initial directory information. A common nmap command for initial AD reconnaissance, as shown on screen, targets these crucial ports and leverages scripts to provide a rich initial dataset. A frequent mistake here is to run nmap without these specific AD-focused scripts, which means you'd miss out on a wealth of valuable initial enumeration data that could quickly point you towards potential vulnerabilities. Always remember to tailor your nmap scans to the specific context of Active Directory.

Once we've identified potential Windows servers and their open ports using nmap, our next step is to move to more targeted enumeration, especially from a Linux-based attack machine. For this, enum4linux is an indispensable tool. It's specifically designed to enumerate information from Windows and Samba hosts, leveraging various techniques to extract valuable data. One of its core methods is NetBIOS enumeration, which can reveal hostnames, domain names, and workgroup information. More powerfully, enum4linux employs RID cycling, a technique that iterates through Relative Identifiers to guess valid user accounts. It also utilizes the Security Account Manager Remote (SAMR) protocol to enumerate users and groups. Running enum4linux -a against a target IP, as shown on screen, will attempt to perform all available enumeration techniques, often revealing extensive lists of users, groups, and shared resources. While this can sometimes be a noisy operation, it's an excellent first pass for gathering critical intelligence. For example, using enum4linux -U specifically targets user enumeration, which is a significant step forward for potential password spraying or brute-force attacks. Identifying valid usernames is a cornerstone of many AD attack vectors, making enum4linux a vital tool in your arsenal.

While nmap and enum4linux provide valuable initial insights, the real power of Active Directory enumeration comes from direct interaction with the LDAP service. LDAP, or Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, is the primary protocol used to query and modify the AD database, offering access to a vast amount of information. On Linux, ldapsearch is your go-to command-line tool for this. To use it effectively, you'll need to know the base Distinguished Name, or DN, of the domain, which is typically derived from the domain name itself. For example, for a domain named corp. local, the base DN would be dc equals corp,dc equals local. As you see on screen, a basic query can list all user accounts by filtering for objects of class user and requesting specific attributes like s AMAccount Name. You can refine these filters to find specific groups, computers, or users with interesting attributes. For instance, filtering for admin Count equals 1 can reveal administrative users, while service Principal Name equals asterisk identifies users or computers with Service Principal Names, which are prime targets for Kerberoasting attacks. Understanding how to craft precise LDAP filters is crucial for extracting highly targeted intelligence from Active Directory.

For Windows-based attack machines, or once you've established a foothold within a domain, PowerShell becomes an incredibly powerful and often stealthier tool for Active Directory enumeration. The Active Directory module, which can be imported using Import-Module Active Directory, provides a comprehensive suite of cmdlets specifically designed for interacting with AD. These cmdlets, such as Get-ADUser, Get-ADGroup, Get-ADComputer, Get-ADDomain, and Get-ADForest, allow for highly granular and efficient querying of the AD database directly from a Windows host. As you can see in the examples on screen, you can retrieve all user accounts and display selected properties like s AMAccount Name, Description, and Enabled with a simple Get-ADUser command. Furthermore, PowerShell excels at finding specific attributes, such as users with Service Principal Names, which are crucial for Kerberoasting attacks. You can achieve this by filtering for users where Service Principal Name is not null. These PowerShell cmdlets are often preferred in post-exploitation scenarios due to their native integration, which can be less conspicuous than external tools, and their ability to perform complex queries with ease. Mastering PowerShell for AD enumeration is a key skill for any advanced penetration tester.

It transforms a chaotic data dump into an actionable attack map.
